# The Nine Properties of a Citable Passage

A citable passage is answer-first, self-contained, right-sized, specific, evidenced, single-purpose, plainly written, structurally clean, and well-headed. Here is each property with a before→after example — plus an interactive scorer that grades a paragraph you paste.

BBurke AtkersonMarch 27, 2026 2 min read

A citable passage has nine properties: it is answer-first, self-contained, right-sized, specific, evidenced, single-purpose, plainly written, structurally clean, and well-headed. Together they make a passage an engine can lift out of your page and repeat with confidence. Below is each one with a before→after example — and an interactive scorer that grades a paragraph you paste.

Key takeaways

  * ▸Nine properties separate a liftable passage from an ignored one.
  * ▸Answer-first is the biggest lever — Profound: 44% of citations come from the first third of a page.
  * ▸Right-sized means ~120–180 words (SE Ranking); single-purpose means one question per passage.
  * ▸Evidenced and specific passages are safer for an engine to repeat (the credibility pillar).
  * ▸Use the scorer below to catch obvious misses before you publish.

Engines cite passages, not pages — write the sentence you want quoted, and put it first.

## What are the nine properties?

The nine properties of a citable passage are the concrete, checkable traits that make your writing easy for an answer engine to extract. They are the writing-craft expression of extractability, the AEO Canon's third pillar. None is exotic; together they are decisive.

### 1. Answer-first

The complete answer appears in the first sentence, before any context. Profound found 44% of ChatGPT citations come from the first third of a page — lead with the answer or lose the citation.

✕Before

There are several things to consider when thinking about how often you should publish new content for AEO, and the right answer depends on a number of different factors.

✓After

For AEO, publish on a cadence matched to how fast your topic changes: weekly for fast-moving subjects like pricing or tools, monthly for stable evergreen topics. Frequency matters less than keeping time-sensitive pages current.

Why it works · The 'after' answers the question in sentence one; the 'before' promises an answer that never arrives.

### 2. Self-contained

The passage makes complete sense when read entirely on its own — no orphan pronouns, no dependence on the paragraph above.

✓After

SE Ranking found pages with a First Contentful Paint under 0.4 seconds earned about three times more AI citations than slower pages.

Why it works · Specificity is what an engine can quote. A vague claim is a sentence it has to soften; a specific one it can repeat as-is.

### 5. Evidenced

Each meaningful claim carries a statistic, quotation, or named source inline. The Princeton GEO study (arXiv 2311.09735) found quotations lifted visibility ~41%, statistics ~30%, and citing sources ~30%. This is the credibility pillar at the passage level.

### 6. Single-purpose

The passage answers exactly one question. Two questions in one block give the engine a muddy unit; split them so each is independently liftable. This is the core move in turning a page into a Q&A library.

### 7. Plainly written

Sentences are short and direct enough to parse without re-reading. Long, clause- stacked run-ons are hard for a human to follow and hard for a model to lift cleanly.

✕Before

While there are many considerations that go into the process, and despite the fact that the landscape is constantly changing in ways that can be difficult to predict, it is nevertheless generally advisable, in most cases, to lead with your answer.

✓After

Lead with your answer. The landscape changes constantly, but that move works in almost every case.

Why it works · Same point, half the friction. Plain sentences are easier for both readers and engines to extract.

### 8. Structurally clean

No keyword stuffing, no repeated phrases jammed in for density. The GEO study found keyword stuffing reduced AI visibility (~-10%) — the opposite of what writers hope. See does keyword stuffing help or hurt?

### 9. Well-headed

The passage sits under a heading phrased as the question it answers, which both signals the passage's purpose and matches how people query AI. Full method in how to use question-shaped headings.

## Score your own passage

Paste a paragraph and the tool grades it against all nine properties in your browser. It is a heuristic estimate — useful for catching obvious misses, not a substitute for judgment.

Score your passage

Paste a paragraph below. It's scored in your browser against the nine properties of a citable passage — nothing is sent anywhere.

Your nine-point score appears here as you type.

How to read your score

Treat anything flagged red or amber as a prompt, not a verdict. The scorer can't judge whether your answer is correct or genuinely useful — only whether it has the surface traits of a liftable passage. A 9/9 passage that's wrong still won't earn trust; a 7/9 passage that nails the answer often will. Use it to remove friction, then rely on your own read.

## Where this fits in the Canon

The nine properties are how you operationalize extractability and credibility as a writer. Start with the cornerstone, how to write content AI will quote, then go deep on the highest-leverage properties: answer-first sentences, question-shaped headings, and passage length.

## Frequently asked questions

What makes a passage citable by AI?
    Nine properties. A citable passage is answer-first (the answer is in sentence one), self-contained (it makes sense lifted out of context), right-sized (about 120–180 words), specific, evidenced (carries a stat, quote, or source), single-purpose (one question per passage), plainly written, structurally clean (no keyword stuffing), and well-headed (under a question-shaped heading). The more it has, the more liftable it is.

Which property matters most?
    Answer-first. Profound found 44% of ChatGPT citations come from the first third of a page, so leading with the complete answer is the highest-leverage move. The other eight properties make that answer cleaner, safer, and easier to lift, but a buried answer fails before they matter.

How long should a citable passage be?
    Roughly 120–180 words. SE Ranking's analysis associates that range with AI citations — long enough to answer one question completely, short enough for an engine to lift whole. Passages much shorter tend to be thin; much longer tend to cover several questions and get skipped.

Can I test whether my passage is citable?
    Yes — the scorer on this page grades a pasted paragraph against all nine properties using client-side heuristics (nothing is sent anywhere). It is a rough estimate to catch obvious misses, not a guarantee. The surest test is still to read the passage aloud, alone, as the answer to one question.

# Locating Supporting Details

> Why This Matters for Nursing: A physician's order reads "administer 500 mg every 8 hours." A patient chart lists an allergy in one line among fifty. Nursing is full of moments where the right answer is written down somewhere and your job is to find the exact stated fact — quickly and without misreading it. Locating supporting details is that skill.

## What You Need to Know

A supporting detail is a specific piece of information stated directly in the text — a fact, number, name, date, definition, or example. Locating-details questions ask you to go back to the passage and retrieve information that is explicitly written there.

You are not interpreting, inferring, or summarizing. You are finding what the text actually says.

### The Key Distinction

> Main idea = the big point of the whole passage. Supporting detail = one specific fact that backs up or fills in that point. Inference = something the text implies but never states.

Locating-details questions live entirely in the "it's written right there" world. If you cannot point to the exact sentence that proves your answer, you have the wrong answer.

* * *

## 🧠 Memory Trick

> "Point to the proof."
> 
> For a locating-details question, you must be able to put your finger on the exact word, number, or sentence in the passage that gives the answer. No sentence = no answer.
> 
> Watch for the signal phrase: "According to the passage / text / label..." — that phrase is the test telling you the answer is stated somewhere; go find it.

* * *

## How to Locate a Supporting Detail

### Step-by-Step:

  1. Read the question first — identify the exact thing being asked for (a number? a name? a definition? a side effect?).
  2. Pull out the keyword — the unusual noun or term in the question (e.g., "pulse rate," "half-life," "night differential"). That keyword is your search target.
  3. Scan, don't re-read — sweep the passage for that keyword or its synonym instead of re-reading every word.
  4. Read the full sentence around the keyword — details often hide in a clause ("...except in emergencies").
  * "Reasonable alternatives" → listed ✓
  * "The provider's home address" → not listed ✗ → this is the answer

Answer: The provider's home address — the only element the passage never mentions.

* * *

## 💡 Pro Tips

  * Let the keyword do the work. Scanning for one distinctive term is faster and more accurate than re-reading the whole passage.
  * Read one sentence past your keyword. Details and their exceptions often sit in the next clause or sentence.
  * Beware synonym swaps. The right answer often paraphrases the passage ("elevated" for "high"). Match meaning, not just exact words.
  * On charts, labels, and forms: the answer is a specific cell, line, or value — locate it precisely rather than estimating.
  * If you can't point to the proof, it's not the answer. Every locating answer has a home sentence.

## ⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  * Choosing a "true in real life" answer. If the passage doesn't state it, it's wrong — even if it's medically correct.
  * Grabbing the first keyword match. The passage may mention the term twice; read the sentence that actually answers the question.
  * Missing the "NOT/EXCEPT" flip. Skipping the word "NOT" turns three wrong-for-this-question choices into traps.
  * Confusing a detail with the main idea. A locating question wants one specific fact, not the passage's overall point.
  * Over-reading into an inference. If you find yourself reasoning "well, that probably means...", you've left locating territory.

* * *

## Quick Reference

### Locating a Detail

Step  | Question to Ask
--- | ---
1. Read the question  | What exact fact is being asked for?
2. Grab the keyword  | Which distinctive term do I search for?
3. Scan the passage  | Where does that term appear?
4. Read the full sentence  | What does the text actually say?
5. Match a choice  | Which option restates the passage?

### Signal Phrases That Mean "Go Find It"

  * "According to the passage / text / label / chart..."
  * "The passage states that..."
  * "Based on the information given..."
  * "Which of the following is mentioned...?"

### Red Flags for Wrong Answers

  * True in real life but not stated in the passage
  * Adds a fact, number, or reason the text never gives
  * Matches the keyword's first appearance, not the answering sentence
  * Ignores a "NOT" or "EXCEPT" in the question

## How to recognize locating a specific detail questions

  * The prompt asks what the text states or indicates about a detail.
  * Answering means pointing to a specific line, not summarizing.
  * Some stems contain NOT or EXCEPT, reversing what counts as correct.
  * Choices paraphrase the passage, some faithfully and some not.

## Why students miss these

Everything you need is on the page, so the difficulty is precision, not knowledge. A choice can echo the passage's words while changing a qualifier, a number, or who did what. NOT and EXCEPT prompts invert the whole task, and skimming past them flips your answer to a wrong one. Matching each choice to an exact line, and re-reading the stem for a reversal, is what keeps a faithful paraphrase from losing to a distorted one.
